description:
Found by measuring the goal program, which is what the epic's SIGNAL exists for.

    fnp walk(<<_c, r :: binary>>, n), do: walk(r, n + 1)
    fnp walk(_b, n), do: n

    walk(<a 40-byte binary>, 0)
      81 bitstring allocations, 22,176 bytes

Two allocations per byte, and 22 KB to look at 40. Every `<<c, r :: binary>>`
step allocates a fresh copy of the REMAINDER, so a scan over n bytes copies
n + (n-1) + ... bytes. Quadratic, in the one operation every parser performs.

In Erlang a sub-binary is a few words -- an offset and a length into the
original -- and matching a tail is O(1) with no copy. That is what makes
byte-oriented scanners idiomatic there, and it is the shape fz's surface invites
by supporting the same patterns.

MEASURED ON THE GOAL PROGRAM: decoding a 68-byte JSON document costs 435
bitstring allocations and 71,600 bytes. The document contains about ten bytes of
string content. Almost all of that is tail copies from the scan, not the strings
being built.

I tried the obvious library-level fix first -- count a run, then take one slice
instead of appending per byte -- and it came out slightly WORSE (437
allocations), because counting the run is itself a traversal and the traversal
is the cost. That is the evidence that this is a runtime data-model issue and
not something a library can work around.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND JSON: fz-5xp.14 (String) is entirely byte scanning, and
every function in it will be quadratic until this changes. So will any user
program that parses anything.

DONE = matching a binary tail produces a reference into the original rather than
a copy, with the goal program's allocation golden re-measured -- the drop is the
point. Needs: a sub-binary representation the GC understands (it must keep the
original alive), and a decision about when to flatten one back into a copy,
which is the usual space-leak trade in that design.

WATCH OUT: `procbin` already exists for shared large binaries, so some of the
machinery for "a binary that points at bytes it does not own" is in place.
title: Matching a binary tail COPIES it, so every byte scanner is quadratic
